Now, we need to compute the probabilities for each tornado type that we have classified. This can be done quite simply by dividing the number of tornadoes that we have classified to each tornado type by the total number of tornadoes. The results are summarized in the following table:


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Tornado Type      | Number of Tornadoes|Probability |
|:-----------------|-------------------:|:-----------|
|Coastal to Inland |                 417|0.93%       |
|Inland to Coastal |               16535|36.96%      |
|Other             |               27786|62.11%      |


:::
:::


As shown, there are far fewer coastal-to-inland tornadoes compared with inland-to-coastal and other tornadoes. This relatively small amount reflects the strict requirement that the tornado must start within a short distance of the coast to be classified in this category.


::: {.cell}

:::


Lastly, we estimate the probability that a tornado is strong enough to lift a shark, conditional on it being coastal-to-inland. According to @fisheriesWhiteSharkNOAA2025, great white sharks can weigh up to 4,500 lbs. Similarly, @HowMuchDoes reports that the average car weighs approximately 4,419 lbs, suggesting that great white sharks are of comparable mass to cars. From @CanCarBe2025, EF3 tornadoes are “likely to toss cars and trucks,” whereas EF4 tornadoes are “very likely to toss cars many feet.” This indicates that at least an EF4 tornado would be required, since a sharknado would require sharks not only to be lifted, but also transported a substantial distance inland rather than merely displaced. These sharks must be pulled out of the water as well, which adds to the wind speed necessary. This gives all the more reason to rule out EF3 tornadoes and only consider EF4 and EF5. To compute this probability, we first have to define the number of tornadoes for each combination of magnitude $m$ and movement type $t$, call this $N_{m,t}$. The probability of a tornado having magnitude $m$ given movement type $t$ is the number of tornadoes with magnitude $m$ and movement type $t$ divided by the total number of tornadoes with movement type $t$.

$$
P(\text{Magnitude} = m|\text{Movement} = t) = \frac{N_{m,t}}{\sum_{m} N_{m,t}}
$$ For our specific probability we are interested in this probability where m = 4 or 5, and t = coastal to inland.

Computing this probability we get:

$$
\frac{1 + 0}{417} 
\approx 0.24\%
\quad
(1 \text{ from magnitude 4},\ 0 \text{ from magnitude 5})
$$
The one tornado that we have seen to satisfy our conditions for a sharknado occurred on April 4, 1966. The location where it first touched down is below: 


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](results_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


While this one tornado satisfies the defined conditions, it relies on strong assumptions. A shark would need to be present along the coastline at the moment of formation, and EF4 winds would truly need to be capable of lifting it from the water. If either assumption fails, this case is excluded, leaving a 0% probability of sharknados in the observed data.
